def:
A family of specifications from NVM Express defining a storage interface: controller registers or properties, paired submission and completion queues, a command format and command sets, independent of the transport that carries them (PCIe, RDMA, TCP).
Kid version: the rulebook for how the teacher writes request slips to the librarian and how answers come back.
Where used: SSD drivers, controller firmware, fabrics targets, analyzers' NVMe decode layer.
Common confusion: NVMe is not PCIe; NVMe over PCIe is only one transport.

Storage media that keeps its contents when power is removed: NAND flash, 3D XPoint-class media, battery-backed DRAM and others. In NVMe specifications the word names the media behind a namespace and the NVM Command Set (Read, Write, Flush...).
Kid version: a notebook that remembers what you wrote even after the lights go out.
Where used: NVM subsystem, NVM Command Set, NVM Sets.
Common confusion: NVM is the media class; NVMe is the interface; the NVM Command Set is one of several NVMe command sets.

A storage device built from semiconductor memory (almost always NAND flash) plus a controller that runs a flash translation layer, error correction and a host interface such as NVMe, SATA or SAS.
Kid version: a library with no moving shelves, just millions of tiny electric boxes.
Where used: everywhere from laptops (M.2) to data centres (U.2, EDSFF).
Common confusion: "SSD" says nothing about the interface; a SATA SSD and an NVMe SSD speak entirely different protocols.

Non-volatile memory organised as pages (read/program unit, typically 4–16 KiB) grouped into erase blocks (hundreds to thousands of pages). Pages cannot be overwritten in place; a block must be erased first, and each block survives a limited number of program/erase cycles.
Kid version: notebook pages written in pen: to reuse a page you must tear out and bleach the whole chapter.
Where used: the media behind almost every SSD.
Common confusion: the host's LBA is not a NAND page; the FTL maps between them.

Controller firmware that maps host logical block addresses to physical NAND locations, writes out-of-place, performs garbage collection and wear levelling, and hides erase-before-write from the host.
Kid version: the librarian's secret index that says which shelf each book is really on today.
Where used: SSD firmware; its behaviour explains write amplification and latency spikes.
Common confusion: the FTL is invisible to NVMe and PCIe traces; you infer it from latency and logs, never see it directly.

A layered, packet-based, point-to-point serial interconnect specified by PCI-SIG: physical lanes, a data link layer (ACK/NAK, flow control) and a transaction layer (memory, I/O, configuration and message requests, and completions).
Kid version: a super-fast private road between buildings, with trucks, receipts and traffic rules.
Where used: GPUs, NICs, SSDs, accelerators.
Common confusion: PCIe knows nothing about NVMe commands; it carries memory reads and writes that NVMe happens to use.

The part of the host that connects the CPU and memory subsystem to the PCIe hierarchy: it originates configuration requests, turns CPU loads and stores into TLPs, and turns device DMA TLPs into memory accesses.
Kid version: the school's main gate where every road to the outside world starts.
Where used: enumeration, MMIO, DMA, AER reporting.
Common confusion: the RC is not a single chip on modern systems; it lives inside the CPU package and contains one or more root ports.
Abbreviation for Root Complex. In course trace tables "RC" marks requests issued by the host (CPU MMIO writes and reads) rather than by the device.

A PCIe function at the leaf of the hierarchy that requests or completes transactions on its own behalf, using a Type 0 configuration header. An NVMe SSD's controller is exposed as a PCIe endpoint function.
Kid version: a house at the end of the road.
Where used: every device that is not a root port, switch port or bridge.
Common confusion: an endpoint is a function, not a physical card; one card can expose many endpoint functions (multi-function, SR-IOV).
Abbreviation for Endpoint. Do not confuse with the TLP EP bit, which marks a poisoned TLP.

A downstream-facing PCIe port of the root complex; it appears to software as a PCI-to-PCI bridge (Type 1 header) and owns the link to the first device or switch below it. Its Link Status, AER and DPC registers are often where host-side link evidence lives.
Kid version: one of the gates in the school wall, each with its own road.
Where used: lspci topology, AER root error status, link training.
Common confusion: errors reported by the root port may be about the device below it, not the port itself.
Abbreviation for Root Port. In the course lab system the root port is 0000:00:01.1 (Requester ID 0x0009).

The address of a PCIe function inside one PCI segment: 8-bit bus, 5-bit device, 3-bit function, written like 01:00.0 (Linux adds the segment/domain: 0000:01:00.0). The same 16 bits form the Requester ID and Completer ID in TLPs.
Kid version: street, house number, and room.
Where used: lspci, sysfs paths, TLP headers, AER messages.
Common confusion: bus numbers are assigned by enumeration and can change between boots or after hot-plug.

A configuration-space register through which a function requests an address window (memory or I/O, 32- or 64-bit, prefetchable or not); software sizes it by writing all ones and reading back, then programs the assigned base. NVMe controller registers live in the memory window of BAR0 (BAR0/BAR1 as a 64-bit pair).
Kid version: the house asks the town for a mailbox address, and the town assigns one.
Where used: enumeration, MMIO, analyzers that decode NVMe by address.
Common confusion: the BAR holds an address, not the registers themselves.

Accessing device registers with ordinary CPU load and store instructions to addresses inside a BAR window; the root complex turns each access into a Memory Read or Memory Write TLP. NVMe doorbell writes are MMIO writes (posted).
Kid version: the device's control buttons appear as if they were desk drawers in the classroom.
Where used: register programming, doorbells, MSI-X tables.
Common confusion: MMIO is CPU→device; DMA is device→memory. Both are memory TLPs on the wire.

A device reading or writing host memory itself, without the CPU copying data, by issuing Memory Read and Memory Write requests (bus mastering). NVMe controllers use DMA to fetch SQEs, move data via PRPs/SGLs, post CQEs and (with MSI-X) signal interrupts.
Kid version: the librarian walks into the classroom and puts the books on the table directly.
Where used: every NVMe data transfer.
Common confusion: DMA addresses are often IOVAs translated by an IOMMU, not physical addresses.

The PCIe transaction-layer packet: a 3- or 4-DW header (Fmt, Type, length, requester/completer IDs, tag, address or routing), optional data payload and optional ECRC. Memory, I/O, configuration, message requests and completions are all TLPs.
Kid version: a truck with a shipping label and maybe some cargo.
Where used: every PCIe transaction; the main object in analyzer traces.
Common confusion: a TLP is not an NVMe command; one NVMe command produces many TLPs.

A small packet (6 bytes on the wire before framing in non-flit modes) exchanged between the two ends of one link only, never forwarded: Ack, Nak, flow-control (InitFC, UpdateFC), power-management and vendor-specific types.
Kid version: the receipt slips the two drivers hand each other at the end of one road.
Where used: reliability, credit return, link power entry.
Common confusion: DLLPs do not cross switches and carry no transaction data.

exp: Link Training and Status State Machine
def:
The physical-layer state machine each port runs to detect a partner, bit- and symbol-lock, negotiate width and speed, equalise, and manage low-power and recovery states: Detect, Polling, Configuration, L0, Recovery, L0s, L1, L2, Hot Reset, Disabled, Loopback.
Kid version: the steps two walkie-talkie users follow before talking: Can you hear me? Which channel? Louder? OK, talk.
Where used: link bring-up, speed changes, error recovery.
Common confusion: Recovery is normal for speed changes; it is only a symptom when it repeats.

A DLLP from the receiving end of a link confirming that every TLP up to and including a given sequence number arrived with good LCRC; the transmitter then frees those TLPs from its replay buffer. One Ack may cover many TLPs.
Kid version: "Got trucks 1 to 7, thanks."
Where used: data link layer reliability.
Common confusion: an Ack is a per-link delivery receipt, not an end-to-end completion and not an NVMe completion.

A DLLP saying a TLP arrived corrupted (bad LCRC) or out of sequence; it carries the last good sequence number, and the transmitter replays every unacknowledged TLP after it. Each Nak is logged as a correctable error (Bad TLP at the receiver).
Kid version: "Truck 8 was smashed, send 8 onwards again."
Where used: link-level retry.
Common confusion: a few Naks are recovered automatically; a steady stream signals a signal-integrity problem.

The PCIe data link layer retry mechanism: every TLP gets a 12-bit sequence number and an LCRC, is kept in the replay buffer until acknowledged, and is replayed on Nak or when the replay timer expires. Rollover of the replay counter forces the link into Recovery.

An optional PCIe extended capability that classifies errors as correctable, uncorrectable non-fatal or uncorrectable fatal, keeps per-error status and mask bits, logs the header of the offending TLP, and lets the root port collect error messages and interrupt the OS.
Kid version: an incident book where each road keeps a list of what went wrong and the truck's label.
Where used: Linux pcieport AER driver messages in dmesg, sysfs AER counters.
Common confusion: AER records PCIe errors only; an NVMe command failure is reported in the CQE status, not by AER.

An interrupt mechanism in which a device signals by writing a data value to a system-specified address (a Memory Write TLP); configured through the MSI capability, with up to 32 vectors that must be allocated as a contiguous power-of-two block.
Kid version: instead of ringing a shared bell, the librarian drops a numbered note in the teacher's tray.
Where used: older or simpler devices; NVMe allows MSI as an alternative to MSI-X.
Common confusion: MSI is not MSI-X; vector count, table location and masking differ.

An interrupt mechanism with up to 2048 independently addressed and maskable vectors, described by a table in a BAR (address, data, vector control per 16-byte entry) and a Pending Bit Array. NVMe drivers typically map one vector per completion queue.
Kid version: every answer box gets its own private doorbell into the teacher's room.
Where used: NVMe completion signalling; seen in traces as an MWr to the 0xFEEx_xxxx range on x86.
Common confusion: the interrupt is just a Memory Write TLP; ordering with the preceding CQE write matters.

Abbreviation for Submission Queue: a circular buffer of 64-byte commands written by the host and read by the controller.
Kid version: the request box.
Common confusion: the host owns the tail, the controller owns the head.

A circular queue of fixed-size command entries (64 bytes for NVMe over PCIe I/O queues by default, set by CC.IOSQES) in host memory or the controller memory buffer. The host writes entries and advances the tail doorbell; the controller fetches from the head and reports its head position back in each CQE (SQHD).
Kid version: a round tray of request slips; you add at one end, the librarian takes from the other.
Where used: every NVMe command.
Common confusion: the SQ entry is fetched by device DMA; the doorbell write carries only the new tail index.

Abbreviation for Completion Queue: a circular buffer of 16-byte completion entries written by the controller and consumed by the host.
Kid version: the answer box.
Common confusion: several SQs may share one CQ.

A circular queue of completion entries (16 bytes each over PCIe) written by the controller via DMA; the host detects new entries by the phase tag, processes them, and writes the CQ head doorbell to release slots. Optionally tied to an interrupt vector.
Kid version: the answer tray the librarian fills.
Where used: every completed command.
Common confusion: completions can arrive out of submission order; match them by CID and SQ ID.

The submission queue with ID 0, used for admin commands (Identify, Create I/O queues, Get Log Page, Set Features...). Over PCIe its base address is programmed into the ASQ register (offset 28h) and its size into AQA before CC.EN is set.
Kid version: the request box for the head office, not for ordinary books.
Where used: controller initialisation and management.
Common confusion: ASQ is both the queue and the register holding its base address.

The completion queue with ID 0, paired with the admin SQ; its base address goes in the ACQ register (offset 30h) and its size in AQA. Completions for admin commands and Asynchronous Event Requests are posted here.
Kid version: the head office's answer box.
Where used: initialisation, async events.
Common confusion: ACQ must be physically contiguous over PCIe; I/O CQs may be too, depending on CAP.CQR.

A 16-bit value the host puts in Command Dword 0 of each SQE; together with the SQ ID it uniquely identifies an outstanding command, and the controller echoes it in the CQE.
Kid version: the ticket number on a request slip.
Where used: matching completions to commands, Abort, error log entries.
Common confusion: CIDs are only unique per SQ, and reusing one before its completion is consumed is a host bug.

A 32-bit identifier in Command Dword 1 naming the namespace a command targets. Valid IDs start at 1; 0 means "not used" and FFFFFFFFh is the broadcast value meaning all namespaces where the command allows it.
Kid version: which section of the library the request is for.
Where used: I/O commands, Identify, Get Log Page, Format.
Common confusion: /dev/nvme0n1's "n1" is the Linux namespace instance, usually but not necessarily equal to the NSID.

A 64-bit pointer to a memory page (sized by CC.MPS) used to describe data buffers. PRP Entry 1 may have a page offset; later entries must be page-aligned. Over two pages, PRP Entry 2 points to a PRP list.
Kid version: a list of table numbers where the books should be put.
Where used: NVMe over PCIe data pointers.
Common confusion: "physical" means as the device sees it, often an IOVA behind an IOMMU.

A data-pointer format made of 16-byte descriptors (data block, bit bucket, segment, last segment, keyed data block...) that can describe arbitrary byte-aligned buffers. Optional for I/O over PCIe (reported in Identify Controller SGLS), required for NVMe over Fabrics.
Kid version: a treasure map that can point anywhere, with any size of pile.
Where used: fabrics, large or fragmented buffers.
Common confusion: PSDT in CDW0 selects PRP vs SGL; mixing them up corrupts data silently.

The index of a fixed-size logical block in a namespace (e.g. 512 B or 4 KiB, chosen by the LBA format); commands address data as Starting LBA + Number of Logical Blocks.
Kid version: page numbers of a giant book, regardless of where the paper is kept.
Where used: Read, Write, DSM, ZNS.
Common confusion: LBA 0 of a 4 KiB-format namespace is 8 times bigger than LBA 0 of a 512 B namespace; always check LBADS.

An NVMe I/O command set (revision 1.5 in the 2026 set) that divides a namespace into zones written sequentially from a write pointer and reset as a whole, moving data placement and garbage collection decisions toward the host.
Kid version: notebook chapters you may only write from front to back, then erase as a whole.
Where used: hyperscale storage, log-structured software.
Common confusion: ZNS is not SMR HDD, though both are zoned; ZNS adds Zone Append and zone resource limits.

An NVMe I/O command set (revision 1.4 in the 2026 set) in which the host stores and retrieves values by key (Store, Retrieve, Delete, Exist, List) instead of by LBA.
Kid version: asking for "the red dragon book" by name instead of by shelf number.
Where used: object and key-value stores.
Common confusion: the device indexes keys itself; there are no LBAs in a KV namespace.

An NVMe command set (revision 1.3 in the 2026 set) exposing memory inside the NVM subsystem as memory namespaces that hosts and computational programs can read and write, typically used with Computational Programs.
Kid version: a workbench inside the library where the librarian's helpers can lay out books.
Where used: computational storage.
Common confusion: SLM is not CMB or HMB; it is addressed through namespaces and commands.

The NVM Express specification (revision 2.2 in the 2026 set) for out-of-band management of NVMe devices from a BMC over MCTP (SMBus/I2C or PCIe VDM) and in-band via NVMe-MI Send/Receive commands: health polling, inventory, configuration.
Kid version: the building caretaker checking the library's lights and temperature without disturbing readers.
Where used: servers, enclosures, fleet management.
Common confusion: out-of-band management does not use the host's NVMe queues.

Carrying the NVMe command model over a network transport (RDMA, TCP, Fibre Channel) using capsules instead of memory-resident queues and doorbells; defined in the NVMe Base Specification plus transport specifications.
Kid version: sending request slips to a library in another town by post.
Where used: disaggregated storage, storage arrays.
Common confusion: no PCIe exists between host and remote controller; a fabrics trace contains PDUs or RDMA operations, not TLPs.

A PCIe card form factor that plugs into a standard PCIe slot (CEM connector), used for high-power or high-capacity SSDs.
Kid version: a big library extension bolted onto the school's slot.
Where used: workstations, servers.
Common confusion: slot width (x16 mechanical) can exceed the electrical lanes wired; check negotiated width.

A 2.5-inch drive form factor using the SFF-8639 connector, carrying up to four PCIe lanes (or SAS/SATA), hot-pluggable in server bays.
Kid version: a book-sized drive that slides into a drawer.
Where used: enterprise servers.
Common confusion: U.2 is a connector/form factor, not a protocol; U.3 changes the pin-out for tri-mode backplanes.

A small card form factor (e.g. 2280 = 22 mm × 80 mm) with keyed edge connectors; M-key modules carry up to four PCIe lanes for NVMe, B-key modules may carry SATA or two PCIe lanes.
Kid version: a stick of gum that holds a whole library.
Where used: laptops, desktops, boot drives in servers.
Common confusion: an M.2 slot may be wired for SATA only; the same form factor can host different protocols.

exp: Enterprise and Data Center Standard Form Factor
def:
A family of SSD form factors (E1.S, E1.L, E3.S, E3.L) designed for dense, hot-swappable, well-cooled data-centre storage, mostly carrying x4 (or wider) PCIe links.
Kid version: library drawers shaped to fit a server rack perfectly.
Where used: hyperscale and enterprise servers.
Common confusion: the form factor does not fix the PCIe generation or the NVMe revision.

A PCI-SIG extended capability that lets one physical function (PF) create many lightweight virtual functions (VFs), each with its own configuration space, BARs and Requester ID, so VMs can be given direct device access.
Kid version: one library building split into many small rooms, each with its own front door.
Where used: virtualised NVMe SSDs, NICs.
Common confusion: SR-IOV only creates PCIe functions; NVMe controller resources for each VF are managed separately (Virtualization Management).

A full-featured PCIe function with the SR-IOV capability, which configures and manages its virtual functions.
Kid version: the main room of the library that controls the side rooms.
Where used: SR-IOV setup (sriov_numvfs in sysfs).
Common confusion: resetting the PF affects all its VFs.

A lightweight PCIe function created by a PF through SR-IOV; it has its own Requester ID and BAR space but shares physical resources and some configuration fields with the PF.
Kid version: a side room with its own door but the same plumbing.
Where used: assigned to VMs via VFIO.
Common confusion: a VF's Vendor ID/Device ID registers read as FFFFh; identity comes from the PF's SR-IOV capability.
One full-duplex PCIe signalling path: a transmit differential pair and a receive differential pair. Links are built from 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 lanes, and bytes of each packet are striped across them.

The point-to-point connection between exactly two PCIe ports, made of one or more lanes, trained by the LTSSM to a common width and speed. Data link layer reliability (Ack/Nak, flow control) operates per link.

The number of lanes a link actually trained to (x1, x2, x4, x8, x16), reported in the Link Status register as Negotiated Link Width. It can be lower than both ports' maximum when lanes fail or are not wired.

The data rate per lane a link is currently running at (2.5, 5.0, 8.0, 16.0, 32.0, 64.0 or 128.0 GT/s), shown as Current Link Speed in Link Status and by lspci -vv as LnkSta. Compare with LnkCap to detect a downtrained link.
Two conductors carrying opposite-polarity copies of a signal; the receiver measures the difference, rejecting common-mode noise. Each PCIe lane uses one pair per direction.

The 100 MHz reference clock from which PCIe transmitters and receivers derive their bit rate. Systems may use a common clock, separate clocks with or without spread-spectrum clocking, depending on platform design.

Series capacitors on each transmit line that block DC between devices, allowing different common-mode voltages. Receiver detection during the LTSSM Detect state relies on sensing the load behind these capacitors.
The physical-layer circuit that converts parallel data to a high-speed serial bit stream and back, including clock recovery and equalisation.
Receiver circuitry that extracts timing from transitions in the incoming bit stream so bits can be sampled at the right moment; it needs enough transitions, which encoding and scrambling guarantee.
Two-level signalling carrying one bit per unit interval; used by PCIe generations 1 through 5.

Four-level signalling carrying two bits per unit interval; PCIe 6.0 (64 GT/s) and 7.0 (128 GT/s) use it to double the data rate without doubling the symbol rate, at the cost of smaller eyes and a higher raw error rate that FEC corrects.
Half the symbol rate: the highest fundamental frequency a signal toggling every unit interval produces (8 GHz for 16 GT/s NRZ). Channel loss is usually specified at this frequency.
Line code used by PCIe 1.x and 2.x: every 8-bit byte is sent as a 10-bit symbol, guaranteeing DC balance and transitions but costing 20% of the raw bit rate (efficiency 80%).
Line code used by PCIe 3.0 to 5.0: 128 scrambled bits are sent with a 2-bit sync header that marks a data or ordered-set block, giving about 98.46% efficiency.
In PCIe 6.0 and later flit mode, the fixed-size 256-byte unit in which TLPs, DLLPs, CRC and FEC bytes are packed; error detection and retry operate on flits rather than individual TLPs.
Redundant bytes that let a receiver correct some errors without retransmission. PCIe 6.0 flit mode uses a lightweight FEC plus CRC and retry because PAM4 has a much higher raw bit error rate.

Billions of symbols (unit intervals) per second on one lane. For NRZ one transfer carries one raw bit, so 16 GT/s = 16 Gbit/s raw before encoding; usable bytes per second depend on encoding and protocol overhead.

Shorthand for the maximum per-lane rate defined by a base specification revision: Gen1 2.5 GT/s, Gen2 5.0, Gen3 8.0, Gen4 16.0, Gen5 32.0, Gen6 64.0, Gen7 128.0 GT/s. Each generation remains backward compatible with lower speeds.

Errored bits divided by total bits transferred. PCIe NRZ links target 10<sup>-12</sup> or better at the receiver; PAM4 generations accept a higher raw BER (order 10<sup>-6</sup>) and rely on FEC and retry.

XOR-ing data with a pseudo-random sequence from a linear-feedback shift register so the bit stream has enough transitions and a spread spectrum; both ends run identical scramblers, reset by specific ordered sets.

Shaping the transmitted signal (pre-shoot and de-emphasis presets) and filtering the received one (CTLE, DFE) to compensate channel loss. For 8 GT/s and above PCIe defines an equalization procedure in the LTSSM Recovery state with phases 0 to 3.

The handshake in Recovery.Equalization where ports exchange preset and coefficient requests through training sets until each receiver reports acceptable signal quality. Failure causes fallback to a lower speed.
One of a set of predefined transmitter equalisation settings (P0 to P10 in PCIe 3.0–5.0) combining pre-shoot and de-emphasis, requested by the link partner during equalization.
A receiver analog filter that boosts high frequencies to undo channel loss; its gain is one of the knobs tuned during equalization.
A receiver equaliser that subtracts the estimated inter-symbol interference of previously decided bits from the current sample.

A protocol-aware physical-layer extension device that fully recovers and retransmits the signal, participating in link training and equalization on both sides; it is invisible to software but adds latency and its own failure modes.
An analog signal amplifier/equaliser placed in a channel to extend reach; unlike a retimer it does not recover the clock or take part in the protocol.
The ability of a port to accept lanes connected in reverse order (lane 0 to lane N-1), discovered during the Configuration state, easing board routing.
Automatic correction by a receiver when the D+ and D- conductors of a differential pair are swapped, detected in the Polling state from inverted training sets.
A PCIe 4.0+ mechanism that lets software ask a receiver to move its sampling point in time and voltage and report errors, measuring how much eye margin remains without external test equipment.
A sideband signal from the platform that holds a device in fundamental reset while power and clock stabilise; deasserting it starts link training.
An optional sideband signal a device uses to request or release the reference clock, used by L1 PM substates to let the platform stop REFCLK.
An optional sideband signal a device asserts to request that main power be restored from a low-power system state (alternative to an in-band beacon).
A physical-layer control sequence sent on all lanes, never part of a TLP: training sets (TS1, TS2), Electrical Idle (EIOS), EIEOS, SKP, FTS and, at 8 GT/s and above, SDS.
A training ordered set carrying link and lane numbers, supported data rates, and equalization fields; exchanged in Polling, Configuration and Recovery to establish the link.
A training ordered set sent after a port has seen enough TS1s, confirming that the proposed parameters are agreed before moving to the next LTSSM state.
Sent by a transmitter just before it enters electrical idle (for example on entering L0s, L1 or before a speed change).
A low-frequency pattern sent to help a receiver detect exit from electrical idle and, at 8 GT/s and above, to establish block alignment.
Inserted periodically so receivers can compensate for small clock frequency differences between the two ends by adding or removing SKP symbols in their elastic buffers.
Ordered sets used to re-establish bit and symbol lock when leaving L0s; the number needed (N_FTS) is advertised during training.

exp: Start of Data Stream ordered set
def: At 8 GT/s and above, marks the transition from ordered-set blocks to a data stream of TLPs and DLLPs.
A transmitter state with no differential signalling, used in low-power link states and before speed changes; entry is announced by EIOS.
The first LTSSM state, in which a transmitter checks for a receiver termination on each lane; lanes without a partner are excluded.
The LTSSM state where ports exchange TS1/TS2 to achieve bit lock and symbol lock and correct polarity, at 2.5 GT/s. Not to be confused with completion polling in software.
The LTSSM state that agrees link width, lane numbering and link number using TS1/TS2 with PAD fields replaced by real values.
The normal operational link state in which TLPs and DLLPs flow; the data link layer reports DL_Active.

The LTSSM state used to retrain an active link: to change speed, perform equalization, exit L1, or recover from errors such as replay-counter rollover. Repeated entry is a classic sign of a marginal link.
A low-latency, per-direction standby link state entered under ASPM when a transmitter is idle, exited with FTS ordered sets.

A deeper link power state with both directions idle; entered under ASPM or when the device goes to D3hot, exited through Recovery. L1 PM substates (L1.1, L1.2) save more power by turning off more circuits.
L1.1 and L1.2: refinements of L1 in which common-mode voltages (L1.2) and possibly the reference clock (via CLKREQ#) are turned off, trading exit latency for power.
Link states with main power removed: L2 keeps auxiliary power for wake-up, L3 is fully off. Entered through the L2/L3 Ready handshake before power is cut.
A reset propagated in-band through training sets with the Hot Reset bit, usually triggered by setting Secondary Bus Reset in a bridge; resets everything below the link without removing power.
Setting the Link Disable bit in a downstream port's Link Control register takes the link to the Disabled LTSSM state; clearing it retrains the link, which acts like a reset for the device below.
A test state in which the follower port echoes received symbols back to the leader, used for bit error testing and compliance.
An LTSSM substate in which a transmitter sends a compliance pattern for electrical measurements, entered when a test load is detected but no training partner responds.
The data link layer state reached after flow-control initialisation succeeds; only then may TLPs be exchanged. The Data Link Layer Link Active bit in Link Status reflects it where supported.
A 12-bit counter the data link layer prepends to every TLP (non-flit modes) so the receiver can detect lost or duplicated TLPs and Acks can refer to them.
A 32-bit CRC computed by the data link layer over the sequence number and TLP and checked hop by hop; a mismatch causes a Nak and a Bad TLP correctable error.
An optional 32-bit CRC appended to a TLP by its originator (TD bit set) and checked by the final receiver, protecting the TLP through switches; failures are uncorrectable ECRC errors.
Transmitter storage holding every sent TLP until an Ack covers its sequence number, so it can be resent on Nak or timeout. Its size bounds how many unacknowledged bytes a link can have in flight.
A timer started when a TLP is sent; if no Ack or Nak arrives before it expires, all unacknowledged TLPs are replayed and a Replay Timer Timeout correctable error is logged.

A 2-bit counter of consecutive replays of the same TLPs; when it rolls over (four replays without progress) the link is retrained through Recovery and REPLAY_NUM Rollover is logged as a correctable error.

The credit-based mechanism in which a receiver advertises buffer space (header and data credits for posted, non-posted and completion traffic) and a transmitter sends a TLP only when enough credits are available, so TLPs are never dropped for lack of buffer.
InitFC1 and InitFC2 DLLPs exchanged after the physical link comes up to advertise initial credits for each traffic class; completing this handshake brings the data link layer to DL_Active.
A DLLP that returns flow-control credits as the receiver frees buffer space; missing or delayed UpdateFCs starve the transmitter.
An independent set of buffers and flow-control credits on a link, allowing traffic classes to be isolated; most systems use only VC0.
A 3-bit TLP header field labelling a transaction's class of service, mapped to a virtual channel; ordering rules apply within a TC. Almost all NVMe traffic uses TC0.

The combination of the Fmt and Type header fields that identifies a TLP as memory read/write, I/O read/write, configuration read/write (Type 0 or 1), message, completion with or without data, or atomic operation.
The 3-bit field in TLP header byte 0 (non-flit) giving header size and data presence: 000b 3DW no data, 001b 4DW no data, 010b 3DW with data, 011b 4DW with data, 100b TLP prefix.
A non-posted TLP requesting data from a memory address; it is answered by one or more CplD completions carrying the same Tag and Requester ID. NVMe controllers issue MRd to fetch SQEs and write data.
A posted TLP carrying data to a memory address, with no completion. Doorbell writes, CQE posts, read-data DMA and MSI-X interrupts are all MWr TLPs.

The TLPs that answer non-posted requests: CplD returns read data, Cpl (no data) acknowledges a non-posted write or reports an error status (UR, CA, CRS). Routed back by Requester ID and matched by Tag.
Non-posted TLPs that access configuration space, routed by bus/device/function. Type 0 targets a function on the local bus; Type 1 is forwarded by bridges toward a subordinate bus.
A posted TLP used for in-band signalling without an address: error messages (ERR_COR, ERR_NONFATAL, ERR_FATAL), legacy INTx assert/deassert, power management, vendor-defined messages and others.
A request that receives no completion: memory writes and messages. The sender's job is finished once the data link layer has delivered it; there is no end-to-end confirmation that it was consumed.
A request that must be answered by a completion: memory reads, I/O and configuration reads and writes, atomic operations. Each consumes a tag and is subject to completion timeout.
The TLP a completer returns for a non-posted request, carrying a completion status, byte count, lower address and possibly data. A PCIe completion is unrelated to an NVMe completion queue entry.
A 3-bit field in a PCIe completion: Successful Completion (000b), Unsupported Request (001b), Configuration Request Retry Status (010b), Completer Abort (100b).
A completion status (and error type) meaning the completer does not support the request, for example a memory read to an address outside any BAR, or any request when Memory Space Enable is off.
A completion status meaning the completer understood the request but could not complete it because of a violation of its own programming model or an internal error.
A completion status a function returns to configuration requests while it is still initialising after reset; the root complex may retry automatically. Prolonged CRS shows up as slow enumeration.

A requester-assigned number in non-posted requests that, combined with the Requester ID, forms the Transaction ID used to match completions. 8-bit tags give 256 outstanding requests; 10-bit tags allow 1024 and flit mode extends further.

An extension (PCIe 4.0 onward) allowing up to 1024 outstanding non-posted requests per requester, needed to sustain high bandwidth over high-latency paths; both requester and completer path must support it.
The Device Control enable that lets a function use all 8 tag bits (256 tags); without it a requester is limited to 5-bit tags (32 outstanding requests).

The 16-bit Bus/Device/Function of the function that issued a request, carried in request TLP headers and copied into completions so they can be routed back. The IOMMU uses it to select translation tables.
The Bus/Device/Function of the function that generated a completion, carried in the completion header.
Requester ID plus Tag: the unique key for an outstanding non-posted request; a completion is matched to its request by Transaction ID.

exp: First DW BE / Last DW BE
def: 4-bit fields in memory, I/O and configuration request headers selecting which bytes of the first and last DWORD are actually read or written, so transfers need not be DWORD-aligned.
The 10-bit TLP header field giving payload length in DWORDs (1 to 1024, where 0 encodes 1024). It must not exceed MPS for writes or MRRS for read requests.
A completion header field giving the remaining bytes needed to satisfy the read request, including this completion's payload; with Lower Address it lets the requester reassemble split completions.
A completion header field holding the low address bits of the first byte returned, used to place data and to check RCB alignment of split completions.

A TLP whose EP (error poisoned) bit is set to indicate its data is known bad, for example because of an uncorrectable memory error upstream. The receiver must not use the data and logs a Poisoned TLP Received error.
Header bit indicating an ECRC digest is appended to the TLP.
TLP header bits carrying Relaxed Ordering, No Snoop and ID-Based Ordering hints that relax ordering or cache-coherence requirements for a transaction.
An attribute permitting a TLP to pass earlier posted writes in the same direction, improving throughput when software does not depend on that order; must be enabled in Device Control.
An attribute telling the root complex that the transaction need not be snooped in CPU caches, used when software manages coherence itself.
An attribute allowing TLPs from different requesters to pass each other, since ordering normally only matters within one requester's stream.

The producer-consumer rules for which TLP classes may pass which: notably, posted writes must not pass posted writes, and read completions must not pass posted writes in the same direction (unless relaxed). This guarantees that an NVMe CQE write followed by an MSI-X write is seen in order.

The largest TLP data payload a function may send or must accept, set in Device Control (128 to 4096 bytes) and normally programmed to the smallest value supported along the path. Not to be confused with NVMe CC.MPS (memory page size).
The largest amount of data a function may request in one memory read TLP, set in Device Control; larger NVMe data transfers are split into several read requests.
The address alignment (64 or 128 bytes) on which a completer may split a read's completions; except for the first and last, split completions end on RCB-aligned addresses.

An uncorrectable error a requester logs when a non-posted request's completion does not arrive within the programmed timeout range (Device Control 2). For an NVMe device this often means its DMA read of host memory was never answered.
An error logged when a completion arrives whose Transaction ID matches no outstanding request, often after a timeout already retired the request or because of misrouting.
A TLP that violates format rules (length exceeding MPS, inconsistent fields, crossing a 4 KiB boundary...); it is a fatal-by-default uncorrectable error and the TLP is discarded.
A memory request must not cross a naturally aligned 4 KiB address boundary; requesters split transfers accordingly, which is one reason NVMe DMA appears as many TLPs.
Non-posted TLPs (FetchAdd, Swap, CAS) that perform read-modify-write at the completer atomically; optional, used by accelerators more than storage.
Optional DWORDs preceding a TLP header (non-flit mode) carrying extra information such as PASID; local prefixes stay on one link, end-to-end prefixes travel with the TLP.
In PCIe 6.0 flit mode, optional additional header DWORDs carrying information (such as byte enables or PASID) that non-flit TLPs put in other fields or prefixes.
Forwarding of memory and I/O TLPs by switches and bridges based on the address windows programmed in their Type 1 headers.
Forwarding of configuration requests, completions and some messages by bus/device/function, using bridges' secondary and subordinate bus numbers.
A message by which a device tells the platform how much read/write service latency it can tolerate, letting the platform choose deeper power states.
A PCIe capability letting a device request translations from the IOMMU and cache them in its own Address Translation Cache, then send pre-translated requests.
An identifier attached to a request (prefix or OHC) that selects a process address space in the IOMMU, enabling shared virtual addressing between a device and user processes.
A PCIe capability that encrypts and integrity-protects TLPs between two ports or end to end, keyed via SPDM; part of the confidential-computing stack with TDISP.
A DMTF protocol for device authentication, measurement and key exchange, carried over PCIe DOE or MCTP; used to establish IDE keys and attest device identity.
A PCIe extended capability providing a mailbox in configuration space for exchanging structured data objects such as SPDM messages.

A PCI-SIG protocol for assigning a device interface (for example a VF) securely to a trusted execution environment, locking its configuration and attesting its state. NVMe 2.4 adds a TDISP information package reporting controller state.

The per-function register space (256 bytes PCI-compatible plus up to 4 KiB extended in PCIe) holding identification, command/status, BARs and capability structures, read and written with configuration requests.

A memory-mapped window in which every function's 4 KiB configuration space appears at an address computed from bus, device, function and register offset; the root complex turns accesses there into configuration TLPs.

The process in which firmware or the OS walks the PCIe hierarchy with configuration reads, discovers functions, assigns bus numbers to bridges, sizes and assigns BARs, and enables decoding and bus mastering.
The 8-bit number of a PCIe bus segment, assigned during enumeration; each link below a bridge or switch downstream port is a new bus.
The 5-bit device field of a BDF. On a PCIe link below a downstream port the device is normally number 0 (unless ARI is used).
The 3-bit function field of a BDF (0–7, or 0–255 with ARI). A multi-function device exposes several functions sharing one link.
A capability that reinterprets the 5-bit device and 3-bit function fields as one 8-bit function number, allowing up to 256 functions on one device, which SR-IOV needs for many VFs.
The configuration header layout for endpoints: identification, command/status, six BARs (paired for 64-bit), subsystem IDs, expansion ROM BAR, capabilities pointer and interrupt fields.

The configuration header layout for bridges, root ports and switch ports: primary, secondary and subordinate bus numbers, memory and prefetchable windows, bridge control (including Secondary Bus Reset) and two BARs.

The first two 16-bit configuration registers identifying a function's manufacturer (PCI-SIG assigned) and product. A read of FFFFh usually means no function is present or the device has dropped off the bus.

A 24-bit configuration register (base class, sub-class, programming interface) describing a function's type. NVMe controllers report 01h/08h/02h: mass storage, non-volatile memory controller, NVM Express.
A configuration register whose bits enable I/O space decode, Memory Space Enable, Bus Master Enable, SERR# reporting and Interrupt Disable (INTx). Clearing Bus Master Enable stops all device DMA.
The Command register bit that permits a function to issue memory and I/O requests (DMA, MSI/MSI-X). With it clear an NVMe controller cannot fetch commands or post completions.
The Command register bit that makes a function respond to memory requests in its BARs; with it clear, MMIO to the NVMe registers returns Unsupported Request.
A configuration register reporting the capabilities-list presence, interrupt status and legacy error bits such as Received Master Abort, Received Target Abort and Detected Parity Error.

A linked list of capability structures in the first 256 bytes of configuration space (PCI Power Management, MSI, MSI-X, PCI Express capability...), starting at the Capabilities Pointer; each entry has an ID and a next pointer.

A capability structure in extended configuration space (offset 100h and above) with a 16-bit ID, version and next offset: AER, SR-IOV, ACS, Device Serial Number, L1 PM Substates, Secondary PCIe, Physical Layer 16/32 GT/s, DOE and others.

The capability structure holding PCIe-specific registers: Device Capabilities/Control/Status (MPS, MRRS, error reporting enables), Link Capabilities/Control/Status (speed, width, ASPM, retrain), Slot registers and their "2" extensions.
PCIe capability register setting Max Payload Size, Max Read Request Size, Extended Tag enable, Relaxed Ordering and No Snoop enables, error reporting enables, and Initiate Function Level Reset.

PCIe capability registers describing what a port can do (max speed and width, ASPM support), what software asks of it (ASPM control, Retrain Link, Link Disable) and what the link actually is (current speed and width, training, DL active).
An extended capability holding a 64-bit unique device identifier, useful to correlate a PCIe function with inventory records.
A device with one upstream port and several downstream ports, each appearing as a PCI-to-PCI bridge, that forwards TLPs by address or ID routing and adds latency and its own error domains.
A port facing toward the root complex (upstream) or away from it (downstream). Each link has one of each; a switch has one upstream and several downstream ports.
The software model for root ports and switch ports: a Type 1 function with bus numbers and address windows that decides which TLPs to forward.
An endpoint built into the root complex with no link of its own, so it has no link registers or LTSSM.

Adding or removing a device while the system runs, signalled through slot registers (presence detect, attention button, power control) or surprise removal; the OS must enumerate or tear down drivers accordingly.
An uncorrectable error a downstream port reports when its link goes down unexpectedly (not through a requested disable or reset), typical of a removed drive or a dead link.
A capability that, on an uncorrectable error below a downstream port, automatically disables the link to contain the fault so corrupted data does not propagate; software then recovers the link.
DPC extended with RP PIO error handling and logging in root ports, so the root port can contain errors from CPU-initiated (programmed I/O) requests as well.

A capability on switch and root ports controlling whether peer-to-peer TLPs may be routed directly between downstream ports or must be redirected upstream; used to isolate devices assigned to different VMs (IOMMU groups).

A reset of a single PCIe function initiated by setting Initiate Function Level Reset in Device Control; it resets the function's internal state without retraining the link. For an NVMe controller it is a controller-level reset from the PCIe side.
PCIe's umbrella term for cold reset (power applied), warm reset (power stays, PERST# asserted) and hot reset (in-band). Fundamental reset means cold or warm.
A bit in a bridge's Bridge Control register that triggers a hot reset of the link and everything below it.

PCI Power Management device states D0 (on), D1, D2 and D3hot (software-visible, configuration still accessible) and D3cold (main power removed); transitions are controlled through the PM capability and platform.
Hardware-autonomous entry of a link into L0s or L1 when idle, enabled per link in Link Control; saves power but adds exit latency to the next transaction.
A message a device sends to request a wake-up or report a power-management event, handled by the root port's PME service.
Emulated level-triggered interrupt lines (INTA#–INTD#) signalled in PCIe by Assert_INTx/Deassert_INTx message TLPs. Shared and slow; NVMe drivers use them only as a fallback.
A table in a BAR, located via the MSI-X capability's Table BIR and offset, with one 16-byte entry per vector: Message Address (lower and upper), Message Data and Vector Control (mask bit).
An MSI-X structure in a BAR with one bit per vector, set when a masked vector has a pending interrupt so it can be delivered after unmasking.
A signal that makes the CPU suspend normal flow and run a handler. For NVMe over PCIe it is normally an MSI-X Memory Write that tells the host a completion queue has new entries.
The per-core x86 interrupt controller; MSI/MSI-X writes to the 0xFEEx_xxxx address window are delivered to a LAPIC as interrupts.
Combining several completions into one interrupt, by threshold count or time; NVMe exposes it as the Interrupt Coalescing feature (aggregation threshold and time), trading latency for CPU efficiency.
The set of CPUs allowed to handle an interrupt; Linux NVMe maps queue interrupts to CPUs so completions are processed near their submitter.

A PCIe error recovered automatically by hardware with no data loss (Receiver Error, Bad TLP, Bad DLLP, Replay Timer Timeout, REPLAY_NUM Rollover, Advisory Non-Fatal...). Logged and reported with ERR_COR; a rising rate signals a degrading link.

A PCIe error that affects a specific transaction but leaves the link usable (for example Completion Timeout, Unsupported Request, Poisoned TLP); reported with ERR_NONFATAL; software may retry the transaction.
A PCIe error that makes the link or device unreliable (Data Link Protocol Error, Surprise Down, Malformed TLP, Receiver Overflow...); reported with ERR_FATAL and usually requiring a reset.
A correctable physical-layer error (8b/10b or framing errors, block alignment problems) detected by a receiver; often the earliest sign of signal-integrity trouble.
A correctable error recorded when a received TLP has an LCRC error or wrong sequence number; the receiver sends a Nak.
A correctable error recorded when a DLLP fails its 16-bit CRC; the DLLP is discarded.
The case where an uncorrectable-type error (such as UR or completion timeout) is reported as correctable because the agent judges it was handled, for example by the requester.
An uncorrectable error recorded when a received Ack/Nak refers to a sequence number that makes no sense (not outstanding); default severity fatal.
An uncorrectable error when a transmitter sends more than the advertised credits allow, indicating a flow-control bug.
An uncorrectable error for violations of the flow-control protocol, such as advertising credits beyond permitted limits.
Error message TLPs a function sends upstream to report a detected error of each severity; the root port records the source's Requester ID and may interrupt the OS.
AER registers capturing the header of the TLP associated with the first uncorrectable error, so software can see the type, address and requester involved.
An AER field identifying which uncorrectable status bit was set first, important when several errors accumulate before software reads them.
Root port AER registers recording the Requester ID of the function that sent the most recent ERR_COR and ERR_FATAL/NONFATAL messages.
AER registers that suppress reporting of chosen errors (mask) and choose whether an uncorrectable error is fatal or non-fatal (severity). Masked errors may still set status bits.
A message TLP type whose contents are defined outside the base specification; MCTP over PCIe uses VDMs to carry management traffic such as NVMe-MI.

Hardware in the root complex that translates device DMA addresses (IOVAs) to physical addresses per Requester ID and blocks unauthorised accesses (Intel VT-d, AMD-Vi, Arm SMMU). A faulting DMA appears in kernel logs as a DMAR/IOMMU fault.
The smallest set of devices the IOMMU can isolate from each other given ACS and topology; VFIO assigns whole groups to VMs.
A Linux framework that exposes a PCIe function's BARs, configuration space and interrupts safely to user space or a VM, using the IOMMU for DMA isolation; used for device passthrough and by SPDK.
Assigning a PCIe function directly to a VM so its driver talks to the hardware without hypervisor emulation; the IOMMU remaps DMA.
An NVMe admin command used with SR-IOV to assign controller resources (queues, interrupts) to secondary controllers and bring them online or offline.
In NVMe virtualization, the primary controller (on the PF) manages flexible resources and secondary controllers (on VFs) receive them.
The pciutils command listing PCI functions; -tv shows topology, -vvv decodes capabilities (LnkCap/LnkSta, DevCtl, AER), -xxxx dumps raw config space. Reading extended space needs root.
The pciutils command for reading and writing individual configuration registers. Writes can hang or crash a system; reading with it is safe, writing is an expert-level operation.
The Linux virtual file system under /sys exposing kernel objects: /sys/bus/pci/devices/<BDF>/ (config, resource, current_link_speed, aer_dev_*), /sys/class/nvme/, /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/.
Prints the kernel ring buffer: driver probe messages, NVMe timeouts and resets, AER reports, IOMMU faults. Timestamps are kernel time and messages can be rate-limited or lost.
The systemd journal reader; journalctl -k shows kernel messages persisted across boots (when persistent storage is configured), useful after a crash or reboot.

The standard Linux user-space tool for NVMe: nvme list, id-ctrl, id-ns, smart-log, error-log, get-feature, show-regs, and admin passthrough. Some subcommands (format, sanitize, fw-commit) destroy data or change device state.

The in-kernel NVMe host stack: nvme-core implements the command model, namespaces and multipath, the nvme (PCI) module implements the PCIe transport (queues, doorbells, PRPs, interrupts), and nvme-fabrics/nvme-tcp/nvme-rdma implement fabrics hosts.
The Linux driver bound to root ports and switch ports that hosts port services: AER, DPC, PME and hot-plug.
The Linux block layer design with per-CPU software queues mapped onto hardware queues, matching NVMe's many submission queues.
The Linux kernel structure describing a block I/O (target device, starting sector, list of memory segments); bios are merged into requests that the NVMe driver turns into commands.
The Linux subsystem between file systems and block drivers that splits, merges, schedules and tracks I/O requests.
A block layer policy (none, mq-deadline, kyber, bfq) that orders requests; NVMe devices usually run with none.
A Linux asynchronous I/O interface using shared submission/completion rings between user space and the kernel; it can also pass NVMe commands through (uring_cmd) to the character device.
The older Linux asynchronous I/O interface (io_submit/io_getevents), common in fio benchmarks with direct I/O.
File I/O that bypasses the page cache so requests go straight to the block device; required for meaningful device benchmarks and needs aligned buffers.

A widely used storage benchmark tool generating configurable workloads (block size, queue depth, read/write mix, engine) and reporting IOPS, bandwidth and latency percentiles. Write workloads on a raw device destroy data.
A static instrumentation point in the kernel; the nvme driver has tracepoints such as nvme_setup_cmd and nvme_complete_rq that log commands and completions with low overhead via ftrace or perf.
The Linux kernel tracing framework under /sys/kernel/tracing (or debugfs), used to enable tracepoints and function tracing.
A tool capturing block-layer events (queue, dispatch, complete) per request; blkparse renders them, showing where time is spent above the driver.
A high-level tracing language on eBPF for writing short scripts that attach to kprobes and tracepoints, for example to build NVMe latency histograms.
The Linux profiling tool for CPU sampling, hardware counters and tracepoint recording.
An open-source user-space storage toolkit with a polled-mode NVMe driver (via VFIO or UIO) and NVMe-oF target, avoiding kernel interrupts and context switches.
The in-kernel NVMe-oF target, configured through configfs (or nvmetcli), exporting namespaces over TCP, RDMA, FC or the loop transport; ideal for safe fabrics labs.
A Linux NVMe-oF loopback transport connecting the host stack to the local nvmet target without any network or hardware, useful for safe command-level experiments.
The emulated NVMe controller in QEMU, which lets learners exercise drivers, queues and commands in a VM with no risk to real hardware; its behaviour is one implementation, not the specification.
Loadable kernel code (for example nvme, nvme_core, nvme_tcp) whose parameters appear under /sys/module/<name>/parameters.
The Linux device manager that creates /dev nodes and persistent names such as /dev/disk/by-id/nvme-... from device attributes.

The NVMe entity containing one or more controllers, zero or more namespaces, the non-volatile media and the interfaces between them; identified by an NQN. A dual-port SSD is one subsystem with two controllers.
The NVMe interface between a host and an NVM subsystem: it implements registers or properties, queues, command processing and attached namespaces. Over PCIe each controller is a PCIe function.
A controller type that supports I/O queues and command sets (the normal SSD controller), as distinct from administrative and discovery controllers.
A controller type that supports only admin commands for managing an NVM subsystem, with no I/O queues.
An NVMe-oF controller type that only serves the Discovery Log Page, telling hosts which subsystems and transport addresses are available.
A 16-bit identifier, unique within an NVM subsystem, of a controller; reported in Identify Controller and used in namespace attachment and fabrics Connect.

A quantity of formatted non-volatile storage exposed to a host as a range of logical blocks (or keys, zones, memory, depending on the command set), identified by an NSID and attached to one or more controllers.
The admin command (create and delete operations) that allocates and frees namespaces in an NVM subsystem supporting it; a newly created namespace must be attached before use.
The admin command that attaches a namespace to, or detaches it from, a list of controllers; a namespace may be private to one controller or shared.
An allocated namespace exists in the subsystem; it is active on a controller only when attached to it. Identify CNS values distinguish lists of active and allocated namespace IDs.
A 128-bit identifier of a namespace that stays the same across controllers and resets, reported in Identify Namespace.
A 64-bit globally unique namespace identifier reported in Identify Namespace, one of several namespace identifiers alongside NGUID and UUID.
A 128-bit RFC 4122/9562 UUID identifying a namespace, reported through the Namespace Identification Descriptor list.
A UTF-8 string uniquely naming an NVM subsystem or host (e.g. nqn.2014-08.org.nvmexpress:uuid:... or a reverse-domain form); essential in fabrics Connect and discovery.
A value identifying a host to an NVM subsystem, used for reservations and for associating fabrics connections from the same host.
Optional NVMe commands (Register, Acquire, Release, Report) letting hosts coordinate shared-namespace access, similar to SCSI persistent reservations.
A collection of namespaces and unallocated capacity isolated from other sets for performance, part of an endurance group.
A collection of NVM sets sharing wear and endurance management, with its own Endurance Group Information log.
A multipath feature reporting, per ANA group, whether a namespace is optimised, non-optimised, inaccessible, persistent loss or changing on each controller, so hosts choose the best path.
Access to one namespace through several controllers; Linux native multipath presents one block device (nvmeXnY) and selects paths using ANA state.
A value identifying an I/O command set (NVM, Key Value, Zoned Namespace, Subsystem Local Memory, Computational Programs) used in Identify and namespace management.
A specification defining I/O commands and namespace semantics on top of the NVMe Base Specification: NVM, ZNS, KV, SLM, Computational Programs.
A specification mapping the NVMe command model onto a particular transport: NVMe over PCIe Transport (queues in memory, doorbells, PRPs), RDMA Transport, TCP Transport.
A small, fixed location in a device that software reads or writes to observe or control hardware; NVMe controller registers sit in BAR0 over PCIe and are accessed as fabrics properties over NVMe-oF.

The read-only 64-bit register at offset 00h describing MQES, contiguous queues required (CQR), arbitration support, Timeout (TO, in 500 ms units), doorbell stride (DSTRD), NVM subsystem reset support, supported command sets (CSS), boot partition, MPSMIN/MPSMAX, PMR and CMB support.
CAP field giving the maximum I/O queue size the controller supports, as a zero-based value (MQES = 1023 means 1024 entries).
The worst-case time the host should wait for CSTS.RDY to change after setting or clearing CC.EN, in units of 500 ms.
CAP field setting the spacing of doorbell registers: stride = 4 << DSTRD bytes. With DSTRD = 0 the SQ y tail doorbell is at 1000h + (2y × 4) and the CQ y head doorbell 4 bytes later.
The register at offset 08h reporting the NVMe Base Specification version the controller complies with (major, minor, tertiary).
Registers at 0Ch and 10h for masking pin-based and MSI interrupts per vector; not used with MSI-X, which masks in its own table.

The register at offset 14h through which the host enables the controller (EN), selects command sets (CSS), memory page size (MPS), arbitration (AMS), requests shutdown (SHN) and sets I/O queue entry sizes (IOSQES, IOCQES).
The CC bit the host sets to 1 to start the controller after programming AQA, ASQ and ACQ, and clears to 0 to reset it (a controller reset); the controller reflects completion in CSTS.RDY.
The CC field setting host memory page size as 2^(12 + MPS) bytes (0 = 4 KiB); it defines the PRP page size and must lie between CAP.MPSMIN and CAP.MPSMAX.
CC field the host writes to request a normal or abrupt shutdown; the controller reports progress in CSTS.SHST. Skipping it before power loss is counted as an unsafe shutdown.
CC fields giving I/O queue entry sizes as powers of two; for the NVM command set over PCIe they are 6 (64 bytes) and 4 (16 bytes).
The register at offset 1Ch reporting Ready (RDY), Controller Fatal Status (CFS), Shutdown Status (SHST), NVM Subsystem Reset Occurred and Processing Paused.
Set by the controller when it is ready to process commands after CC.EN = 1, cleared after CC.EN = 0 completes. The host must wait for it, up to CAP.TO.

Set by the controller when a fatal internal error occurs that it cannot report through a completion; the host must reset the controller. Reads of all ones (FFFFFFFFh) instead indicate the device is gone, not CFS.
The register at offset 20h; writing the value 4E564D65h ("NVMe") triggers an NVM subsystem reset, which also resets the PCIe link. Optional (CAP.NSSRS).
The register at offset 24h holding the admin SQ and admin CQ sizes (zero-based), programmed before enabling the controller.
An optional region of controller memory exposed in a BAR that the host can use for SQs, CQs, PRP lists or data, reducing DMA round trips; described by CMBLOC and CMBSZ.
An optional region of persistent controller memory exposed through a BAR for byte-addressable access, described by PMR registers.
An optional feature in which the host lends a portion of its DRAM to a (typically DRAM-less) controller, for example for FTL mapping tables; enabled with Set Features.
A controller register the host writes to announce new SQ entries (SQ tail doorbell) or released CQ entries (CQ head doorbell). Over PCIe each write is a posted 4-byte MWr to BAR0 + 1000h + offset.
The doorbell carrying the new tail index of submission queue y; writing it tells the controller that entries up to tail-1 may be fetched.
The doorbell carrying the new head index of completion queue y; writing it frees entries for the controller to reuse. Forgetting it eventually makes the CQ appear full.
An admin command letting a host keep doorbell values in host memory (shadow doorbells with event indexes), so emulated controllers in VMs avoid costly MMIO exits.
A 64-byte command: CDW0 (opcode, fused, PSDT, CID), NSID, metadata pointer, data pointer (DPTR) and command-specific CDW10–CDW15.
A 16-byte completion: DW0 command-specific result, DW1 reserved or command-specific, DW2 SQ Head Pointer and SQ Identifier, DW3 CID, Phase Tag and Status field.

A submission queue and the completion queue it posts to. NVMe allows many SQs per CQ; Linux uses one SQ per CQ per CPU (or CPU group). In RDMA, a queue pair is a different object: the send/receive work queues of a connection.
Either the size of a queue (entries) or, more commonly in performance work, the number of commands outstanding at once. By Little's law, outstanding commands = IOPS × average latency.

Indexes of a circular queue: the producer advances the tail after adding entries, the consumer advances the head after taking them. The queue is empty when head = tail and full when tail + 1 = head (modulo size).
CQE field reporting the controller's current head of the associated SQ, telling the host which SQ slots it may reuse.
CQE field naming the SQ a completed command came from, needed when several SQs share a CQ.

A CQE bit the controller inverts on each pass through the completion queue (starting at 1 after the queue is created zeroed), so the host can tell new entries from stale ones without reading a register.
How the controller chooses which SQ to fetch from next: round robin (required), weighted round robin with urgent priority class (optional), or vendor specific; selected by CC.AMS.
Optional arbitration where I/O SQs are created in high, medium or low priority classes, weighted by the Arbitration feature, plus an urgent class served first.
The 8-bit command code in CDW0 bits 7:0. Admin and I/O opcodes are separate spaces: 02h is Get Log Page on the admin queue but Read on an NVM I/O queue.
Two commands (e.g. Compare and Write) submitted adjacently with FUSE bits so the controller executes them as one atomic unit.

exp: PRP or SGL for Data Transfer
def: CDW0 field selecting whether the data pointer holds PRPs (00b) or SGL descriptors; SGL use requires controller support.
SQE dwords 6–9 describing the data buffer: PRP Entry 1 and PRP Entry 2, or the first SGL descriptor.
SQE dwords 4–5 giving the address of a separate metadata buffer when metadata is transferred separately from data.
Command-specific dwords of the SQE: for Read/Write they hold Starting LBA (CDW10–11), Number of Logical Blocks and flags (CDW12) and more; for Identify, CNS in CDW10.
The 64-bit first logical block address of an I/O command, held in CDW10 (low) and CDW11 (high).
A zero-based 16-bit count in CDW12 of Read, Write and similar commands: NLB = 7 means 8 blocks. Off-by-one errors here are a classic bug.
A Read/Write flag requiring that a write be committed to non-volatile media before completion (or that a read come from media), regardless of volatile write cache.

A controller write cache whose contents may be lost on power failure; reported in Identify Controller and controlled by the Volatile Write Cache feature. When present, Flush or FUA is needed for durability.
Identify Controller field limiting the size of a single command's data transfer, as a power of two in units of the minimum memory page size (0 = no limit). Drivers split larger requests.
NVM command (opcode 02h) transferring logical blocks from a namespace to host memory; over PCIe the controller writes the data with MWr TLPs before posting the CQE.

NVM command (opcode 01h) transferring data from host memory to a namespace; over PCIe the controller fetches the data with MRd TLPs. Completion does not imply media durability unless FUA is set or no volatile cache exists.
NVM command (opcode 00h) requiring that data and metadata in volatile write cache be made non-volatile before completion.
NVM command (opcode 09h) passing a list of LBA ranges with attributes, most often Deallocate (TRIM), telling the controller the data is no longer needed.

Telling the device that LBA ranges no longer hold valid data (DSM Deallocate in NVMe, TRIM in ATA, UNMAP in SCSI), so the FTL can skip copying them during garbage collection. Read-back behaviour is reported by the controller.
NVM command that sets a range of LBAs to zero without transferring data, possibly by deallocating.
NVM command that compares host data with stored data, often fused with Write for atomic compare-and-write.
NVM command that checks the integrity of stored data and metadata without transferring it to the host.
NVM command that copies data from source LBA ranges to a destination range inside the controller, without host data transfer.
Admin command (opcode 06h) returning a 4 KiB data structure selected by CNS: Identify Namespace (00h), Identify Controller (01h), Active Namespace ID list (02h) and many more.
The Identify CDW10 field selecting which data structure to return.

4 KiB structure describing the controller: PCI vendor IDs, serial and model number, firmware revision, MDTS, CNTLID, version, optional admin/NVM command support, number of namespaces, VWC, SGL support, power states and more.

Admin command (opcode 02h) reading a log identified by Log Page Identifier, e.g. Error Information (01h), SMART / Health Information (02h), Firmware Slot Information (03h), plus telemetry, persistent event and command-set-specific logs.

Admin commands (opcodes 09h / 0Ah) that write and read controller features selected by Feature Identifier: number of queues, arbitration, power management, temperature threshold, interrupt coalescing, volatile write cache, APST, host memory buffer and others.
A feature the host sets early to request a number of I/O SQs and CQs; the completion reports how many were allocated, which may be fewer.

term: Create I/O SQ / Create I/O CQ
def: Admin commands (opcodes 01h and 05h) that create I/O queues given an ID, size, base address (or PRP list), and for CQs an interrupt vector; the CQ must exist before an SQ that targets it.

term: Delete I/O SQ / Delete I/O CQ
def: Admin commands (opcodes 00h and 04h) removing I/O queues; SQs must be deleted before the CQ they post to.
Admin command (opcode 08h) asking the controller to abort a command identified by SQ ID and CID; best effort, and the target may still complete normally.

Admin command (opcode 0Ch) the host leaves outstanding so the controller can complete it when an event occurs (error, SMART/health warning, notice such as namespace change); the host then reads the indicated log page. Unrelated to PCIe AER.
Admin command (opcode 18h) that resets the controller's keep-alive timer; mandatory in NVMe-oF so a target can detect dead hosts. Expiry of KATO causes the controller to tear down the association.
Admin command (opcode 80h) that low-level formats a namespace with a chosen LBA format and protection settings, optionally with secure erase; destroys all data in its scope.

Admin command (opcode 84h) that alters all user data in the NVM subsystem so it cannot be recovered (block erase, crypto erase, overwrite), continuing across resets and reporting progress in the Sanitize Status log.
Admin commands to transfer a firmware image into the controller and to activate it in a slot, immediately or at the next reset. Firmware activation behaviour is implementation-dependent.
Admin command starting a short or extended internal diagnostic, with results in the Device Self-test log.
Admin commands carrying security protocol payloads (e.g. TCG Opal) between host and controller for self-encrypting drive management.
A mechanism (Directive Send/Receive and fields in I/O commands) for host hints such as Streams or data placement, letting the host tell the device which writes belong together.
An NVMe feature in which hosts tag writes with placement handles mapped to reclaim units, reducing write amplification without full zoned semantics.
The 15-bit CQE DW3 field holding Status Code (SC), Status Code Type (SCT), Command Retry Delay (CRD), More (M) and Do Not Retry (DNR). All zero means success.
The 3-bit category of a status code: 0h Generic Command Status, 1h Command Specific Status, 2h Media and Data Integrity Errors, 3h Path Related Status, 7h Vendor Specific.
The 8-bit status code interpreted within its SCT, e.g. Generic 00h Successful Completion, 01h Invalid Command Opcode, 02h Invalid Field in Command.
A status-field bit telling the host that resubmitting the same command is expected to fail again; if clear, a retry may succeed.
A status-field bit indicating additional information about the failure is available in the Error Information log.
A status-field value selecting one of the host-configured retry delay times the host should wait before retrying.
Log page 01h: a list of entries with error count, SQ ID, CID, status, parameter error location, LBA, NSID and more, describing recent command errors.

Log page 02h reporting critical warnings, composite temperature, available spare and threshold, percentage used, data units read/written (thousands of 512-byte units), host commands, power cycles, power-on hours, unsafe shutdowns, media and data integrity errors and error log entries.

SMART log bit field flagging conditions such as spare below threshold, temperature out of range, reliability degraded, media read-only or volatile memory backup failure; can trigger asynchronous events.
A vendor-specific estimate of life consumed based on actual use and endurance; 100 means rated life is reached, and values above 100 are allowed.
SMART counters of data transferred, reported in thousands of 512-byte units (one unit = 512,000 bytes), rounded up.
SMART counter incremented when power is lost without a shutdown notification completing.
Host-initiated and controller-initiated log pages carrying vendor-defined internal state for failure analysis; contents are opaque without vendor tools.
A log of significant subsystem events (resets, firmware commits, power-on, thermal excursions...) persisted across power cycles.
A storage location for a firmware image; the Firmware Slot Information log reports the active slot and image revisions.

One of up to 32 controller-defined operating points described in Identify Controller (max power, entry/exit latency, operational or not), selected via the Power Management feature or autonomously via APST.
An NVMe feature in which the controller moves itself to a non-operational power state after a host-configured idle time; can add latency to the next command.
An NVMe power state in which the controller processes no I/O; it returns to an operational state when a command arrives, with the advertised exit latency.

End-to-end data protection metadata (guard CRC, application tag, reference tag) stored with each logical block and checked by the controller and/or host; formats include 16-, 32- and 64-bit guard variants.
Extra bytes per logical block, transferred either contiguous with the data (extended LBA) or in a separate buffer pointed to by MPTR; may hold protection information.
An entry in Identify Namespace describing a supported combination of data size (LBADS, as a power of two), metadata size and relative performance; FLBAS selects the format in use.
The LBA format field giving block size as 2^LBADS bytes: 9 = 512 B, 12 = 4 KiB.
Identify Namespace fields: total size in logical blocks, maximum blocks that may be allocated, and blocks currently allocated. Thin-provisioned namespaces can have NCAP < NSZE.
Presenting a namespace size larger than the capacity actually reserved for it, allocating media only as data is written.
In ZNS, a contiguous LBA range written sequentially at its write pointer, with states such as Empty, Implicitly/Explicitly Opened, Closed, Full, Read Only and Offline.
The next LBA that may be written in a zone; writes not at the write pointer fail.
A ZNS command that writes data at a zone's current write pointer chosen by the controller and returns the assigned LBA in the completion, allowing many outstanding writes to one zone.
ZNS commands to change zone states (open, close, finish, reset, offline) and to report zone descriptors.
Controller limits (Maximum Active Resources, Maximum Open Resources) on how many zones may be active or open at once; exceeding them causes command failures.
An NVMe command set (revision 1.3 in the 2026 set) for loading and executing programs on compute resources inside the NVM subsystem, operating on data in Subsystem Local Memory.
A namespace associated with a compute engine on which programs are executed in the Computational Programs command set.
Code, either device-defined or downloaded, that the Computational Programs command set can activate and execute on a compute engine.
A namespace of Subsystem Local Memory addressed by byte ranges, used as working memory for computational programs.
Optional areas of NVM readable through registers (BPINFO, BPRSEL, BPMBL) before the controller is fully enabled, so a platform can load boot code with minimal driver logic.
An ACPI table, defined by the NVMe Boot specification, through which pre-OS firmware hands NVMe-oF boot connection details to the operating system.
Firmware code supplied with a device or platform that lets pre-OS firmware (UEFI) drive the device, e.g. to boot from NVMe.
A DMTF transport for management messages over SMBus/I2C, PCIe VDM, I3C and others; NVMe-MI messages ride on MCTP.
A service processor on a server board that manages hardware out of band, including polling NVMe drive health via NVMe-MI.
Read-only inventory data (part number, serial, FRU information) stored on a device, accessible through NVMe-MI or the PCI VPD capability.
Low-speed two-wire buses used for sideband management; NVMe-MI uses them via MCTP, and a basic management command over SMBus can read drive status.

Cryptographic algorithms designed to resist attacks by quantum computers. The NVMe 2.4 release updates asymmetric key-exchange algorithms to prepare for PQC (press coverage names NIST FIPS 203/204/205); check the Base 2.4 specification for exact mechanisms.
The NIST post-quantum key-encapsulation standard FIPS 203 (August 2024).

In NVMe 2.4, a virtual NVM subsystem that a physical SSD exposes (for example to a VM), which can be migrated live between devices using a configuration template. Field-level details must be checked in the Base 2.4 specification.

In NVMe 2.4 subsystem migration, a definition (a "blueprint") of the features, identifiers and behaviours an Exported NVM Subsystem exposes, identified by a 128-bit UUID so source and destination match.
NVMe 2.4 controls letting a subsystem cap PCIe bandwidth and IOPS per controller, so multiple tenants share a device predictably.
NVMe 2.4 capability to detect differences between the voltage a platform supplies and what the device receives, with over/undervoltage thresholds, alerts and history.
An NVMe 2.4 capability that returns an NVM subsystem to its as-shipped configuration state; consult the specification for scope and the data it affects.

An NVMe mechanism that prohibits selected commands or feature changes from chosen interfaces; NVMe 2.4 lets lockdown settings persist across reboots and adds separate controls for virtualized environments.
An NVMe 2.4 capability letting hosts specify latency thresholds the device must respect when leaving idle states.
The NVMe-oF unit that carries a command (command capsule: SQE plus optional data or SGLs) or a response (response capsule: CQE plus optional data) across a fabric.
A capsule containing a 64-byte SQE and optionally in-capsule data or additional SGL descriptors, sent from host to controller.
A capsule containing a 16-byte CQE (and possibly data), sent from controller to host.
Write data carried inside the command capsule itself, avoiding a separate data transfer step for small writes; the maximum size is advertised by the controller.
An NVMe-oF-specific command type (opcode 7Fh with a Fabrics Command Type): Connect, Property Get, Property Set, authentication and others.
The Fabrics command that creates an admin or I/O queue association between a host (Host NQN, Host Identifier) and a controller in a subsystem (Subsystem NQN), returning the controller ID.
