Fabrics commands that read and write controller properties (CAP, CC, CSTS...), the fabric equivalent of MMIO register access.
A log returned by a discovery controller listing subsystem NQNs, transport types, addresses and service IDs a host may connect to.
A discovery controller serving a whole fabric (for example in NVMe/TCP environments), where hosts and subsystems register so discovery scales.

The NVMe transport binding over TCP/IP: capsules and data are carried in PDUs over TCP connections, one connection per queue; defined in the NVMe over TCP Transport specification (1.3 in the 2026 set).

In NVMe/TCP, a framed message with a common header (type, flags, header length, data offset, length) and optional digests: ICReq, ICResp, CapsuleCmd, CapsuleResp, H2CData, C2HData, R2T, H2CTermReq, C2HTermReq.
The first NVMe/TCP PDU a host sends on a new connection, negotiating PDU version, digest use and alignment.
The controller's reply to ICReq, confirming parameters such as maximum H2C data size and digest settings.
An NVMe/TCP PDU carrying write data from host to controller, usually in response to an R2T.
An NVMe/TCP PDU carrying read data from controller to host; a flag may indicate success so no separate response capsule is needed.
An NVMe/TCP PDU in which the controller asks the host to send a specific range of write data, controlling buffer usage.
An optional CRC32C over an NVMe/TCP PDU header, negotiated at connection setup, catching corruption that TCP checksums miss.
An optional CRC32C over an NVMe/TCP PDU's data, negotiated at connection setup.
Encryption and authentication of TCP connections; NVMe/TCP supports TLS 1.3 with pre-shared keys to protect data in flight.
The NVMe-oF in-band authentication protocol based on challenge-response with optional Diffie-Hellman exchange, run with fabrics authentication commands after Connect.
Network technology letting one host read or write another host's registered memory without involving its CPU, using queue pairs and memory keys; transports include InfiniBand, RoCE and iWARP.

The NVMe transport binding over RDMA: capsules travel as RDMA SEND messages and data moves by RDMA READ/WRITE using keyed SGLs; defined in the NVMe over RDMA Transport specification (1.3 in the 2026 set).
RDMA over Ethernet (RoCEv2 over UDP/IP), usually requiring a lossless or congestion-controlled network.
RDMA layered on TCP, tolerating ordinary lossy networks.
A switched-fabric network technology with native RDMA, credit-based link flow control and its own management model.
The communication manager used to resolve addresses and establish RDMA connections; NVMe/RDMA exchanges private data during connection setup.
Pinning and registering a buffer with an RDMA adapter, which returns keys (lkey/rkey) allowing local or remote access to it.
A key that authorises a remote peer to access a registered memory region; NVMe/RDMA puts it in keyed SGL descriptors so the target can RDMA READ/WRITE host buffers.
An RDMA send queue and receive queue forming one connection endpoint; NVMe/RDMA maps each NVMe queue to an RDMA QP. Not the same thing as an NVMe SQ/CQ pair.
The NVMe transport over Fibre Channel, defined by INCITS T11 (FC-NVMe) rather than by NVM Express.
The time within which a controller expects a Keep Alive command or other activity before declaring the host lost; set at Connect in NVMe-oF.
The processor chip inside an SSD running firmware for the host interface, FTL, ECC and NAND channel management. Distinct from the NVMe "controller", which is a logical interface.
NAND cells storing 1, 2, 3 or 4 bits by distinguishing 2, 4, 8 or 16 charge levels. More bits per cell lowers cost but reduces endurance and increases read and program latency.
The smallest unit of NAND that can be programmed or read, typically 4–16 KiB plus spare bytes for ECC.
The smallest NAND unit that can be erased, containing many pages (megabytes in modern 3D NAND); the reason in-place updates are impossible.
NAND parallelism units: a channel is a bus to several dies, each die can operate independently, and each die has planes that can work in parallel. SSD throughput comes from keeping many dies busy.
One program and erase of a NAND block; blocks wear out after a rated number of cycles (thousands for TLC, fewer for QLC).

The FTL structure mapping each logical block (or mapping unit, often 4 KiB) to its current NAND location; roughly 1 byte of DRAM per KiB of capacity in common designs, which is why DRAM-less SSDs use HMB.
FTL background work that copies still-valid pages out of partially stale erase blocks so they can be erased and reused; a main source of write amplification and latency spikes under sustained writes.
FTL policy that spreads program/erase cycles evenly across blocks so no block wears out early.
Bytes written to NAND divided by bytes written by the host; garbage collection, metadata and small random writes push it above 1.
NAND capacity beyond what the host can address, giving the FTL free space for garbage collection and reducing write amplification.
Redundancy that lets a decoder correct bit errors; SSDs use strong codes (commonly LDPC) on NAND data. An uncorrectable read becomes an NVMe media error status.
A powerful iterative ECC used in modern SSDs; decoding with soft information takes longer, so worn or aged data shows up as higher read latency before it fails.
Charge disturbance of neighbouring cells caused by repeated reads, which the FTL handles by refreshing (rewriting) affected blocks.
How long NAND keeps data readable without power; it shortens as the cell wears and with higher temperature.
How much data a device can be written before rated wear-out, usually stated as TBW or DWPD over the warranty period.
Rated total host data that may be written over the device's life: TBW = capacity × DWPD × 365 × warranty years (with consistent units).
Rated number of full-capacity writes per day sustainable over the warranty period.
Capacitors and firmware that let an SSD commit cached writes to NAND after unexpected power loss; drives with PLP often report no volatile write cache.
A region of TLC/QLC NAND written in faster single-bit mode to absorb bursts; sustained writes beyond it drop to native speed, a common benchmark surprise.
Small fast memory holding recently used data to avoid slower accesses: CPU caches, the OS page cache, an SSD's DRAM or SLC cache. Each one changes what a measurement means.
Magnetic rotating-disk storage with millisecond seek and rotational latency, where sequential access is far faster than random.
The serial successor of ATA for disks, 6 Gb/s maximum line rate, with a single command queue of 32 entries (NCQ) via AHCI.
The register-level host interface for SATA controllers: one command list of 32 slots per port, designed for disk-era latencies.
The serial SCSI transport for enterprise disks and SSDs, with dual porting and expanders; 12 Gb/s per lane, or 22.5 Gb/s for the "24G" generation.
A command set and architecture model (CDBs, LUNs, sense data) used by SAS, iSCSI, Fibre Channel and USB storage.
The SATA mechanism allowing up to 32 outstanding commands per device, compared with up to 64 K queues of 64 K entries in NVMe.
The time from issuing an operation to its completion. Always state where it is measured (application, block layer, driver, analyzer) because each boundary includes different components.
Data moved per unit time (MB/s, GB/s). Bandwidth often means the theoretical capacity of a link, throughput the achieved rate.
Completed I/O commands per second; throughput = IOPS × transfer size.
Latency at high percentiles (p99, p99.9, p99.99): the slowest requests, which often dominate user-visible performance and expose garbage collection, retries or power-state exits.
The value below which a given percentage of samples fall: p99 latency of 200 µs means 99% of commands finished within 200 µs.
In a stable system, average number in the system L = arrival rate λ × average time in the system W. For storage: outstanding commands = IOPS × average latency.
The fraction of time a resource is busy (ρ = arrival rate × service time for one server). Queueing delay grows sharply as utilization approaches 1.
Decimal versus binary units: 1 GB = 10<sup>9</sup> bytes, 1 GiB = 2<sup>30</sup> = 1,073,741,824 bytes (7.4% larger). Drive capacities use GB; memory and page sizes use KiB/MiB/GiB.
A 32-bit (4-byte) unit. TLP lengths, NVMe command dwords (CDW0–CDW15) and register fields are described in DWORDs.

Byte order of multi-byte values. NVMe data structures and PCIe register contents are little-endian, while TLP headers are drawn and transmitted most significant byte first; mixing these up is a common decoding error.
The processor executing software; in the NVMe flow it builds commands in memory, writes doorbells (MMIO) and handles interrupts.
Volatile main memory where NVMe queues, PRP lists and data buffers live in host systems.
The CPU abstraction that gives each process its own address space mapped to physical pages through page tables; device DMA cannot use process virtual addresses directly.
The data structure that maps virtual pages to physical pages for the CPU MMU, or IOVAs to physical pages for the IOMMU.
The address a device uses for DMA when an IOMMU is active; the IOMMU translates it to a physical address. Addresses seen in PCIe traces on such systems are IOVAs.
A range of addresses with a meaning: CPU physical memory, MMIO windows, PCI configuration space, I/O port space, IOVA space. The same number can mean different things in different spaces.
Data movement between a computer and devices, or the operations that cause it. Also the legacy PCI I/O address space, rarely used by modern devices.
Operating system code that programs a device: for NVMe it enables the controller, creates queues, builds commands and handles completions.
Completing I/O by repeatedly checking the completion queue instead of waiting for an interrupt (Linux poll queues, SPDK); lowers latency at the cost of CPU.

A CPU instruction ensuring earlier memory writes are visible before later ones, e.g. before writing a doorbell the driver must make sure the SQE is in memory; omitting it causes rare, timing-dependent corruption.
Ensuring device DMA sees CPU-written data and the CPU sees device-written data despite caches; x86 root complexes snoop, other platforms may need explicit cache maintenance.
Test equipment that captures link traffic passively through an interposer or probe and decodes it into ordered sets, DLLPs, TLPs and (with configuration) NVMe commands, with precise timestamps.

A board inserted between host slot and device (CEM, U.2, M.2, EDSFF variants) that taps the lanes for an analyzer. It changes the channel and can itself cause training or signal problems at high speeds.
Test equipment that emulates a host or device and generates arbitrary, including illegal, PCIe traffic to test a DUT's responses.
An in-line device that modifies traffic on the fly (corrupting LCRC, dropping Acks, altering fields) to test error handling deterministically.
An analyzer condition (a TLP pattern, error, LTSSM state, or external signal) that marks where to keep the capture, with configurable pre- and post-trigger buffer.
An analyzer setting excluding traffic types (e.g. SKP ordered sets, idle DLLPs) from recording to stretch buffer depth; excluded events are invisible during analysis.
A time-ordered recording of protocol events. In this course every trace is labelled synthetic, real, excerpted, reconstructed or conceptual.
A reference capture of known-good behaviour used to diff against a failing capture to find the first divergence.
The earliest event in a trace or log that deviates from expected behaviour; root-cause work starts there, not at the loudest or latest error.
A test chosen so that competing hypotheses predict different outcomes, so its result eliminates at least one.
The underlying defect whose removal prevents the failure, as opposed to the symptom or proximate trigger; stated with evidence and confidence.
A test added after a fix that would have caught the bug, run continuously to keep it from returning.
Testing against specification requirements: PCI-SIG compliance workshops and Integrators List for PCIe, UNH-IOL and NVMe conformance test suites for NVMe.
Deliberately introducing errors (link errors, malformed commands, power loss, surprise removal) to verify detection, reporting and recovery.
An oscilloscope overlay of many bit periods; the open area (eye height and width) shows signal margin. PAM4 has three stacked eyes.
The device being validated or debugged.
The time attached to a captured event. Analyzer timestamps, kernel timestamps and application timestamps come from different clocks and must be aligned before correlation.
Linking events from different layers (application, block layer, NVMe command, TLP, interrupt, AER) into one causal timeline, using identifiers such as CID, tag, address and time.

In this course, captures taken from PCIe switch-integrated debug or trace facilities (the PEX name is used by a family of PCIe switches) rather than from an external analyzer; formats and fields are vendor-specific.
A ratified version of a specification (e.g. NVMe Base 2.4). Features, fields and requirements can differ between revisions, so every claim should name the revision it relies on.
Normative text states requirements (shall, should, may); informative text explains. Only normative statements define compliance.
Documents that change a ratified specification between revisions (PCI-SIG ECNs, NVM Express ratified TPs and ECNs); they are later folded into the next revision.
The industry consortium that develops and publishes the NVMe specifications at nvmexpress.org.
The consortium that develops PCI Express specifications; the base, CEM and other specifications are available to members.
The PCI-SIG specification for add-in card and slot mechanics and electricals (connector, power, REFCLK, PERST#).
The multi-function connector used by U.2 drives, carrying up to four PCIe lanes plus SAS/SATA and sideband signals.
A variant of the U.2 drive connector pin-out (SFF-TA-1001) that lets tri-mode backplanes host NVMe, SAS or SATA drives in the same bay.
EDSFF form factors: E1.S is a small ruler-like module for 1U servers, E3.S a larger form for 2U servers; both typically carry x4 PCIe and support hot-plug.
Notches on an M.2 edge connector that indicate supported interfaces: M-key for up to x4 PCIe (and SATA), B-key for SATA or x2 PCIe.
Throughput × round-trip latency: the amount of data that must be in flight to keep a path busy. It sets how many tags, credits or queue entries a design needs.
Payload bits divided by line bits for a line code: 8/10 = 80% for 8b/10b, 128/130 ≈ 98.46% for 128b/130b; flit mode has its own fixed overhead for CRC and FEC.
Bytes on the link that are not payload: framing, sequence number, TLP header, ECRC, LCRC, plus DLLPs and ordered sets. Small payloads waste a larger fraction of the link.
Time a request waits before service starts; it grows non-linearly with utilization, which is why latency rises long before throughput saturates.
The performance level an SSD reaches after enough sustained writing that garbage collection is continuously active; fresh-out-of-box results are higher and misleading.
The average of a set of samples and the average squared deviation from it; latency distributions are skewed, so mean alone hides the tail.

The completion TLP (Fmt 010b, Type 01010b) that returns read data for a memory read, configuration read or I/O read; a large read may be answered by several CplDs split on RCB boundaries, each carrying Byte Count and Lower Address.

Four DWORDs in the AER capability that capture the header of the TLP associated with the first reported uncorrectable error (for example the MRd that timed out or the request that got UR), letting software see its type, address, requester and tag.

An AER register in root ports recording that ERR_COR, ERR_NONFATAL or ERR_FATAL messages were received (including "multiple" flags) and whether the first uncorrectable was fatal; paired with Error Source Identification to find the reporting function.

The AER register with one RW1C bit per uncorrectable error type (Data Link Protocol Error, Surprise Down, Poisoned TLP, Completion Timeout, Completer Abort, Unexpected Completion, Receiver Overflow, Malformed TLP, ECRC Error, Unsupported Request, ACS Violation and more); companion Mask and Severity registers control reporting.

The AER register with one RW1C bit per correctable error type (Receiver Error, Bad TLP, Bad DLLP, REPLAY_NUM Rollover, Replay Timer Timeout, Advisory Non-Fatal, Corrected Internal Error, Header Log Overflow); a companion Mask register suppresses reporting.
